cells.tense: You can right now carry a practice through to its completion and put it down clean.
cells.act: learn how it grows by tending it
cells.ask: Pick one skill you're building and tend it like a grower — steady sessions, what it wants changing your method — and notice what it's actually asking for.
cells.core:
With a practice you're building, you can push and hold and then close at the right finish — a set done, a form ended, a session over — without dragging it out. The close is what makes the work whole, and the work reads as whole because of it.

Feed this rather than test it. Tend the thing like a grower, not a commander: keep the same small appointment with it, learn how it grows, and let what it needs change your method. Nothing has to be forced here, and nothing has to be proven. You'll know the difference by how much you have left after.
cells.sheetLine: You can finish a practice cleanly and call it done.
cells.verb: carry out the thing through to its end
cells.place: in the small daily work where a skill is built one repetition at a time

cells.tense: A practice is being pushed before the next step can be earned and the push is running the room.
cells.act: judge it by the discipline, not the mood
cells.ask: At the end of a session, set down what you actually did — sets, minutes, what held — and score the session by that page, not by how the mood felt walking in.
cells.core:
You hold a practice with high command, and lately the command arrives before the work. There's the named drill, done, and then there's a week already plotted, a standard set above what the drill has earned, an outcome braced for before anything has been built to carry it. It feels like rigor from the inside. Beside you it reads as tension tightening a thing that was still growing.

So put the push on paper instead. At the end of a session, set down what actually happened — sets, minutes, what held — and score the session by that page, not by how it felt walking in. That's the discipline answering, not the mood. What's left when the bracing drops is the practice itself, and it does know its own next step.
cells.sheetLine: You're forcing the practice before it has earned the next step.

cells.tense: A practice has gone quiet and the one who stopped attending it is still standing at the door.
cells.act: lay the one step you can see, solidly
cells.ask: Lay out the smallest next step in the practice, in a place you'll actually meet it. Do it once this week, solidly, and no more.
cells.core:
The place where a skill gets built by repetition has gone quiet. There's no argument with it and no claim about it, just a thin patch where attention used to be, and it's been some time now. What's sat down at the door is the person who was going to use it.

This stretch of your life doesn't want great effort or grand feeling — that's the trap here. Lay one visible step, the smallest you can see, and set it where you'll actually meet it. Take that step once this week, solidly, and treat it as the whole job. A low seat comes back through strength, not through being pushed to feel. One step, done, is what gets the current through.
cells.sheetLine: It's gone quiet. Lay the smallest next step and take it once.
cells.verb: carry out the thing through to its end
cells.place: in the small daily work where a skill is built one repetition at a time

cells.tense: A practice is being kept going by a hand that won't write its own name under the work.
cells.act: apprentice yourself to the material thing
cells.ask: Take one small part of the practice and learn it the way a beginner would — fresh hands, no credit — and let what you find arrive as new work, claimed by you.
cells.core:
The practice still runs. The daily repetitions still get made, and the showing up is steady. What has slipped off is the account: what gets built there is carried as the thing that happens, not as something the person in that chair authors. The practice has a keeper, and the keeper is not counting itself in.

So go back to the early form of it. Take one piece of the practice — a single part, one part only — and learn it like an apprentice: fresh hands, no credit, no seniority. Do the small tending of it, watch what it asks for, and welcome what you find as new. What the hands already know gets claimed that way, from the bottom, and the name comes back onto the page.
cells.sheetLine: The practice runs, and you've left your name off it.
cells.verb: carry out the thing through to its end
cells.place: in the small daily work where a skill is built one repetition at a time

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in my draft is that the person has 'stopped' their practice and is keeping an old form alive in its place — the record says the seat is running on empty, not that a specific habit died; a reader could reasonably say nothing has ended, the capacity is simply thin. The ask (lay one step visibly) survives being wrong because it does not depend on a death-diagnosis, just on an empty seat; it is useful either way. The sentence that serves me more than the person is anything about 'the old light' or 'what you used to do' — it is my image, not their record, and I cut it.
